content.text: Lesson 2 Overview

The transition away from extractive industries, though challenging, offers significant opportunities for innovation and sustainable economic growth. However, this shift could lead to job displacement and economic shocks, necessitating strategies to support affected workers.

content.title: Key Concepts
content.intro: Explore foundational ideas from this lesson.

concepts.title: gender gap in energy employment
concepts.body: The gender gap in energy employment refers to the disparity between the number of men and women working in the energy sector, often characterized by fewer women in technical, leadership, and decision-making roles compared to their male counterparts.

concepts.title: just transition workforce programs
concepts.body: Just transition workforce programs are initiatives designed to support workers and communities in transitioning to sustainable jobs and industries, ensuring that the shift to a greener economy is fair and equitable, providing training, resources, and support for those affected by changes in the job market.

concepts.title: skills development ecosystems
concepts.body: Skills development ecosystems refer to interconnected networks of organizations, institutions, and resources that collaboratively support the continuous learning and enhancement of skills among individuals, often tailored to meet the needs of the labor market and promote economic growth.

content.text: According to the International Labour Organization (ILO), efforts to limit global warming could create millions of new jobs globally, but the transition away from fossil fuels may also result in the loss of millions of jobs in the energy sector by 2030. Despite this, recent scenarios suggest that job creation will outpace losses. By 2030, 103 million new jobs could be created under sustainable energy and <ai prompt="Clarify circular economy.">circular economy 💬️</ai> models. In 2022 alone, the global renewable energy sector added 1 million jobs, with solar photovoltaic (PV) leading this growth. Solar PV jobs reached 4.9 million, comprising over a third of the renewable energy workforce, with women holding 40% of these positions.

While this progress is encouraging, the transition must accelerate to address the estimated 78 million jobs at risk. The challenge lies in the limited overlap between fossil fuel and clean energy jobs, both geographically and in terms of job quality. This gap threatens to leave workers behind and could undermine political support for the energy transition.

To counter this, it is essential to leverage the entire clean energy value chain 💬️, such as localizing critical mineral supply chains and fostering downstream activities beyond extraction. This approach can create new jobs and build community support. However, a seamless transition from fossil fuel to clean energy roles is not always feasible. Therefore, supporting broader economic diversification, particularly in countries reliant on single industries, is crucial.

content.title: A: Policy Frameworks and Reskilling Initiatives

content.text:
Effective policy frameworks are key to facilitating the shift to green jobs, and capacity building efforts are necessary to upskill and reskill workers. The green jobs transition requires deliberate action to protect livelihoods and align education and training programs with emerging opportunities. For instance, Egypt’s Technical and Vocational Education and Training II project, a €116 million initiative, supports renewable energy programs across 13 institutions. Similarly, the Philippines’ Green Jobs Act encourages the creation, sustainability, and incentivization of green jobs, while improving workforce development planning.

In crisis settings, the just energy transition 💬️ serves as an investment in long-term stability by fostering local capacities and infrastructure for recovery and development. Countries heavily dependent on energy imports, such as Yemen and Lebanon, demonstrate the potential of sustainable energy to build both resilience and livelihoods. Yemen’s ERRY III joint program, which focuses on upskilling over 1,100 individuals—particularly women—in solar services, and Lebanon’s training programs for women engineers are examples of how targeted initiatives can drive positive outcomes.

content.text: Employment difference by sector between the baseline and 1.5°C Scenario, thousand jobs

The figure illustrates the anticipated shifts in employment across diverse industries by 2050. It shows job losses in coal, oil, gas, and fuel manufacturing sectors, alongside gains in agriculture, basic manufacturing, and electric supply industries.

Just transition planning is critical to ensuring affected workers and communities are adequately supported throughout the process. By promoting inclusive and equitable economic diversification, policymakers can effectively manage the energy transition while advancing sustainable development and social equity.

Worker retraining and skills development programs are crucial in facilitating a smooth transition away from extractive industries. By providing workers with the necessary qualifications for sustainable roles in emerging sectors, these programs ensure that individuals can adapt to changing job markets and contribute to the growth of clean energy industries.

Retraining and skills development programs are pivotal for a smooth transition away from extractive industries. By equipping workers with the qualifications needed for sustainable roles in emerging sectors, these programs help them adapt to changing job markets and contribute to the growth of clean energy industries. Many workers in traditional energy sectors already possess transferable skills. For example, oil and gas workers may transition to offshore wind or carbon capture projects, while coal miners could shift to mining critical minerals 💬️ for low-carbon technologies.

Government assistance and targeted programs are crucial in helping unemployed workers find new opportunities, ensuring job quality, and promoting equitable benefit distribution. Addressing workplace safety, equity, and inclusion also fosters public acceptance of the energy transition.

Labor unions, industry associations, and educational institutions play a collaborative role in supporting retraining efforts. These partnerships facilitate access to training programs, advocate for worker rights, and promote industry-specific certifications, contributing to the effective implementation of just transition strategies.
The sustainable energy transition offers a chance to reduce inequalities in the sector. In Asia alone, an estimated 4.4 million additional engineers will be needed by 2030 to meet renewable energy targets. According to IRENA (2024), women currently make up only 15% of the wind sector workforce but 40% in solar PV in the region. Strengthening human capital to support the transition is an opportunity to increase women's participation in STEM and build a more inclusive workforce across Asia and the Pacific.

The transition to renewable energy necessitates comprehensive workforce development strategies to address the diverse challenges faced by workers from various sectors. While some skills from fossil fuel industries are transferable to clean energy roles, many workers will require targeted upskilling or reskilling to meet the specific demands of new positions. For example, transitioning from oil and gas to offshore wind may involve building upon existing competencies, but additional training is essential to ensure proficiency in the distinct aspects of renewable technologies (IEA, 2024).

A gender-sensitive approach is crucial to ensure an equitable transition. Expanding training opportunities for women, promoting their advancement into leadership roles within the energy sector, addressing risks of gender-based violence, and providing psychological support for all workers are critical components. Such measures not only foster inclusivity but also enhance the sector's capacity to meet evolving challenges by leveraging a diverse and skilled workforce.

content.title: Case Study: North Macedonia
content.subtitle: Building a future-ready workforce: public-private training and mentorship tackling critical skills gaps in key sectors.

content.text:
North Macedonia faced a critical labor market paradox: while unemployment reached 17.8% in 2019—nearly three times the EU average—employers across key industries desperately needed skilled workers (UNDP, 2020). Youth unemployment hit 34.9%, yet companies such as EVN needed 500 electrical fitters immediately, textile manufacturers lacked technicians for new equipment, and construction required 600 specialized workers within a year (UNDP, 2020).

This severe skills mismatch constrained job creation and hindered the country’s economic transition toward EU competitiveness. Against this backdrop, the ‘Bridging the Skills Gap to Create New and Better Jobs’ project emerged as a UNDP initiative funded by the UK’s FCDO. It was implemented between 2020 and 2022 to address these critical shortages through targeted vocational training in the construction, textile, and renewable energy sectors..
The Challenge: A Widening Skills and Employment Divide

Energy: The electricity company EVN urgently needed 500 electrical fitters to maintain operations (UNDP, 2020).

Textiles: A lack of technicians qualified to operate advanced machinery stalled technology adoption (UNDP, 2020).

Construction: The industry, representing 5.4% of GDP, faced a deficit of approximately 600 technicians, threatening development projects (UNDP, 2020, para. 3; (UNDP, 2021).

Furthermore, a national digital skills deficit, with 50% of the population having low digital literacy 💬️, hindered the country's competitiveness in an increasingly technology-driven global economy.

The ‘Bridging the Skills Gap’ project was designed as a multi-sectoral intervention to align workforce skills with labor market needs. It specifically targeted youth, women, and the long-term unemployed.
The core of the intervention was the Future Skills Training Center (FSTC), a public-private partnership with SEEU. The FSTC delivered specialized training in emerging technologies, including:

· Building Information Modeling (BIM) for the construction sector.
· 3D Product Design for the textile industry.
· Hybrid Photovoltaic Collectors for the renewable energy sector.

A second key component was the development of a sustainable mentorship system. In collaboration with the Economic Chamber of Commerce, the project aimed to train 100 mentors within private companies to provide on-the-job guidance for vocational students.

The project’s success was built on a systematic, four-part implementation strategy:

1. Stakeholder Mapping and Engagement: A multi-stakeholder platform was created, bringing together over 186 companies, policymakers, and educators. This platform facilitated direct dialogue, ensuring that training programs were aligned with real-world industry requirements (UNDP, 2021)

2. Skills Assessments and Forecasting: The project conducted three sector-specific skills assessments. These analyses identified critical technology drivers and informed the creation of seven new occupational standards designed to meet future digital demands and promote gender equality (UNDP, 2021).

3. Gender-Responsive Training Design: Based on the assessments, the project developed and delivered training models focused on high-demand skills. The programs were a major success, training 155 people—2.5 times the initial target (UNDP, 2021). An additional 60 individuals were trained through the newly established FSTC. A specific focus was placed on recruiting and training women in high-tech fields to improve their employment and earning potential (UNDP, 2021).

4. Curriculum and Policy Strengthening: The project supported the Ministry of Education and Science in drafting key policy documents. This collaboration led to the adoption of the new Law on Secondary VET Education before the 2021/2022 academic year, creating a legal foundation for modernized vocational training and the FSTC’s continued operation (UNDP, 2021).
Results and Impact

The project delivered measurable outcomes and created a sustainable impact on North Macedonia’s vocational training landscape.

· 6 post-secondary occupational standards developed.
· 6 post-secondary curricula developed.
· 158 individuals enrolled in non-formal VET (due to legal constraints, formal post-secondary model was not implemented).
· A concept on Regional VET Center was prepared and approved by the Ministry of Education and Science.
· 6 private sector representatives participated in the model design.
· 60 trainees (at least 30% women) enrolled in non-formal training.
· 156 candidates completed non-formal training.
Implementation Challenges and Mitigation

While successful, the project navigated several potential challenges inherent in such systemic reforms:
· Delays in the adoption of relevant legislation, such as the Law on Secondary VET Education, hampered timely implementation of new models (UNDP, 2022).
· Rigid bureaucratic structures complicated coordination among ministries, schools, and training centers (UNDP, 2022).
· Building trust and sustained collaboration between government, private sector, and education providers took more time than expected (UNDP, 2022).

· Employer-Led Design: Direct involvement of the private sector is non-negotiable for ensuring curriculum relevance.
· Multi-Stakeholder Collaboration: A formal platform for dialogue between government, industry, and education is crucial for shared understanding and commitment.
· Evidence-Based Planning: In-depth skills assessments and labor market analysis provide the essential data for effective program design.
· Adaptive Legal Frameworks: Embedding training models into national policy and law is fundamental for sustainability and scale.
Key Success Factors:

These were solved by the following solutions:

· Stakeholder mapping identifies key actors across sectors.
· Piloting a multi-stakeholder platform successfully brought together ministries, companies, educational institutions, and development partners to streamline coordination and unblock legislative hurdles.
· The platform facilitated regular dialogue and trust-building, enabling private-sector input into skills assessments and curricula design.
Considerations for Replication

· Contextualize Institutional Arrangements: The PPP model for the FSTC worked in North Macedonia. Other contexts may require different arrangements that align with local governance and educational structures.

· Secure Sustainable Financing: Long-term financial planning must be a core component from the outset, exploring a mix of public, private, and fee-based revenue streams.

· Prioritize Sectors Strategically: Sector selection should be driven by a rigorous analysis of local economic drivers and future growth potential.

· Build Local Capacity: Investment in building the institutional capacity of local partners is essential for successful implementation and long-term ownership.
References

content.title: B: Regional Disparities in Job Creation

content.text:
The energy transition faces a dual challenge: regional disparities in job creation and the concentration of high-quality jobs in developed countries. While employment opportunities in the clean energy sector are growing, they are unevenly distributed across the globe. Developing a sufficiently large and skilled local workforce is imperative in every region, as most energy jobs are tied to the location where installations are developed (IEA, 2023).

China holds a widening lead in renewable energy deployment and dominates equipment manufacturing, creating a significant share of high-quality jobs. The EU and countries such as the United States, India, Brazil are also major installers, working to strengthen domestic supply chains for greater local value creation. However, this concentration of high-quality jobs in developed countries further exacerbates global inequalities, leaving many developing regions behind.
Skilled labor shortages are already evident in the clean energy sector, particularly in construction roles, which account for nearly half of new energy jobs. These shortages limit the availability of workers needed to install clean energy technologies and retrofit buildings.

Despite the growing demand, the number of workers obtaining relevant qualifications is not keeping pace. Vocational training and degrees in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) critical to the energy sector are not growing fast enough to meet this need.

Regions that rely heavily on fossil fuels, such as coal, oil, or gas, will feel the impacts of the energy transition most acutely and will require targeted support. Governments must also address the financial barriers workers face in retraining, while ensuring marginalized communities 💬️ are not left behind.

A just transition requires addressing both global and regional disparities. Socioeconomic factors like income levels, education, and access to training vary widely across regions, and tailored programs are essential to build local capacities. Diversifying local job markets and prioritizing clean energy infrastructure where it’s most needed—not just where it’s easiest to implement—are crucial steps.
Ultimately, addressing these disparities and ensuring the benefits of clean energy job creation are shared more equitably is key to achieving a truly inclusive energy transition.

content.title: C: Gender disparities in the energy sector

content.text:
The energy transition is an opportunity to advance gender equality and support marginalized communities. While renewable energy sectors are already more inclusive, employing 32% of women compared to 22% in the oil and gas industries, significant disparities remain, particularly in leadership roles where women occupy less than 14% of senior positions. To tap into the potential of energy transition, it must be approached with deliberate intent and supported by prioritizing gender equality in every stage of the energy transition—from policy design to workforce development.

The energy sector remains one of the least gender-diverse industries worldwide. Despite women constituting approximately 39% of the global labor force, they occupy only 16% of positions in the traditional energy sector. Moreover, women's wages in this field are nearly 15% lower than those of their male counterparts, and fewer than 15% hold senior management roles (IEA, 2024).

Addressing these disparities is crucial for fostering innovation and achieving a just energy transition. Implementing targeted interventions, such as promoting women's participation in leadership positions and ensuring equitable pay, is essential to rectify existing gender imbalances and unlock the sector's full potential.

Efforts aimed at attracting and retaining more women in the energy sector are indispensable to ensure a fair distribution of the benefits generated by the energy transition. Women are more prone than men to exit both the energy sector and the labor market altogether, underscoring the imperative of dismantling barriers hindering their participation and career progression, as revealed by data from the IEA Gender and Energy Data Explorer (2023).

The impending shifts in labor dynamics driven by climate change carry profound gender ramifications, bearing significant policy implications. Failure to implement measures bolstering women’s engagement in emerging green vocations risks perpetuating existing gender stereotypes, thereby constricting women's access to the burgeoning job market. Hence, the adoption of "gender-transformative" reskilling initiatives spanning various proficiency levels emerges as a requisite to broaden women's pathways to novel employment prospects.

To honor the commitments outlined in the 2030 Agenda and uphold the principle of leaving no one behind, fostering inclusivity emerges as a paramount imperative. It is imperative to integrate women and girls from diverse backgrounds into the transformative journey toward sustainable energy.

While the renewable energy sphere presents fertile ground for women's progression, targeted policies and initiatives are indispensable to combat gender bias and forge environments conducive to inclusivity.

Exemplary initiatives such as Barefoot College's Solar Mamas underscore the transformative power of empowering women and nurturing their interest in STEM careers. Increasing examples of women entrepreneurs in decentralized renewable energy (DRE) and productive uses of renewable energy (PURE) sectors offer lessons for a gender-just energy transition in rural regions. Scholarships, mentorship endeavours, capacity-building initiatives, and access to financing and other enabling conditions stand as linchpins in upskilling women and dismantling gender stereotypes prevalent within the energy sector.

Moreover, the disproportionate burden of unpaid care work borne by women raises formidable barriers to their ingress into clean energy employment and entrepreneurship. Absent supportive policies such as flexible work arrangements or childcare provisions, women risk encountering additional hurdles in accessing clean energy avenues. Addressing these challenges transcends mere gender equality; it is pivotal for optimizing the effectiveness and longevity of clean energy initiatives, as women's insights pave the way for more innovative and inclusive outcomes.

takeaways.title: Reskilling and upskilling are critical for a just energy transition.
takeaways.description: The shift from fossil fuels to renewable energy will create millions of jobs, but it also risks displacing workers in traditional energy sectors. Effective retraining programs, such as those in North Macedonia and Egypt, are essential to equip workers with the skills needed for emerging green jobs. Governments, industries, and educational institutions must collaborate to ensure these programs are inclusive, gender-sensitive, and aligned with local labor market needs.

takeaways.title: Regional disparities in job creation must be addressed.
takeaways.description: While renewable energy job growth is global, high-quality jobs are concentrated in developed regions, exacerbating inequalities. Developing countries, especially those reliant on fossil fuels, require targeted support to build local capacities and diversify economies. Tailored policies and investments in clean energy infrastructure are crucial to ensure that the benefits of the energy transition are equitably distributed.

takeaways.title: Gender equality is a cornerstone of a sustainable energy transition.
takeaways.description: Women are underrepresented in the energy sector, particularly in leadership roles, and face barriers such as wage gaps and unpaid care work. The energy transition offers an opportunity to advance gender equality through targeted initiatives like scholarships, mentorship programs, and flexible work arrangements. Empowering women in STEM and renewable energy sectors not only promotes equity but also drives innovation and long-term sustainability.
